The Double Economy is the term I use for the discrepancy between Greece's macroeconomic success and the lived experience of its population.

Both levels are real, and they are measured in different places. One is the Greece of the headline figures: growth, primary surpluses, bank profits and tourist arrivals. The other is the Greece of the household budget: the rent, the supermarket bill, the water on an island in July. The success story is told from the first; lived reality is felt in the second. As the subtitle of one of the pieces puts it, you cannot see the rent and the supermarket bill from the Acropolis.

The series follows the channels that should carry the success from one level to the other, and asks where they fail to: housing, taxes, the banks and the islands.

## One measure of the gap

The share of people who spend 40% or more of their disposable income on housing, which Eurostat calls the housing cost overburden rate. Greece's rate has come down since 2016, from 40.5% to 26.4% in 2025, but it has been the highest of any EU member state in every year of the series. In 2025 it was more than three times the figure for the EU as a whole, 7.6%.

```{python}
#| label: fig-overburden
#| fig-cap: "Housing cost overburden rate: share of the population living in households that spend 40% or more of their disposable income on housing, Greece and the EU (27 member states), 2016–2025. Source: Eurostat, EU-SILC, dataset ilc_lvho07a, accessed November 2026. EU values for 2016–2018 are Eurostat estimates. Greece's rate was the highest of the member states with data in every year; in 2021 one member state has no figure."
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.style.use("../house.mplstyle")

data = pd.read_csv("data/housing-overburden.csv")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
for area, colour, width in [("EU", "#1F7A8C", 1.8), ("Greece", "#14213D", 2.4)]:
    s = data[data["area"] == area]
    ax.plot(s["year"], s["value"], color=colour, linewidth=width, marker="o", markersize=4)
    first, last = s.iloc[0], s.iloc[-1]
    # the first and the latest value are written on the chart
    for row in (first, last):
        ax.annotate(f'{row["value"]:.1f}%', (row["year"], row["value"]), xytext=(0, 9),
                    textcoords="offset points", ha="center", fontsize=9, color=colour)
    ax.annotate(area, (last["year"], last["value"]), xytext=(14, 0),
                textcoords="offset points", va="center", fontsize=10,
                color=colour, fontweight="bold")

# Greece's latest value is marked in gold: the point the chart is about
g = data[data["area"] == "Greece"].iloc[-1]
ax.scatter([g["year"]], [g["value"]], color="#B8975A", s=46, zorder=3)

ax.set_ylim(0, 45)
years = sorted(data["year"].unique())
ax.set_xlim(years[0] - 0.8, years[-1] + 1.1)
ax.set_xticks(years)
ax.set_xticklabels([str(y) if (y - years[0]) % 3 == 0 or y == years[-1] else "" for y in years])
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, pos: f"{v:.0f}%")
plt.show()
```
